part2_cap_semantics_from_code.source: src/acquisition/retained_observations.py, RetainedAcquisitionStoreV2 class (read directly this milestone, not inferred from prior summaries)
part2_cap_semantics_from_code.cap_value_source: default constructor arg daily_payload_cap_bytes = 1 * GIB_BYTES, not overridden anywhere in supervisord.conf; clamped by max(1_000_000, requested)
part2_cap_semantics_from_code.accounting_period_boundary: NONE. This is a critical correction to a prior-turn assumption: there is no date/calendar-day bucketing, no timezone handling, and no period-key of any kind in the implementation. self._payload_bytes is a plain Python int instance attribute initialized to 0 in __init__ and only ever incremented in _write_budgeted(). The 'daily' in the name is aspirational/documentary only.
part2_cap_semantics_from_code.what_counts_toward_cap: full_payload_bytes = len(canonical(asdict(full))) -- the size of the FULL JSON-encoded RetainedObservation (all fields: response_data, raw_body_base64, response_text, request_payload, response_headers, metadata) computed BEFORE the write decision, in retain() at line ~334-336
part2_cap_semantics_from_code.exact_transition_condition: _is_within_budget(payload_bytes) returns self._payload_bytes + payload_bytes <= self.daily_payload_cap_bytes, checked as a PRE-WRITE gate inside _write_budgeted(). This is evaluated independently on every single retain() call -- it is NOT a one-way sticky flag. A full-payload write can still succeed AFTER the cap has been effectively 'reached' by prior writes, if that specific payload is small enough to still fit within the remaining headroom (self.daily_payload_cap_bytes - self._payload_bytes). This was directly observed in production data (Part 6).
part2_cap_semantics_from_code.disk_reserve_check: usage.free < 10 * GIB_BYTES is checked FIRST, before the cap check, in the same _write_budgeted() call. Both conditions return the identical (False, budget_remaining) shape, so a caller cannot distinguish 'disk floor breach' from 'cap breach' from the return value alone -- only by comparing self._payload_bytes against daily_payload_cap_bytes.
part2_cap_semantics_from_code.pre_cap_representation: full payload (payload_json = full_payload.decode(), the complete canonical JSON of the RetainedObservation dataclass)
part2_cap_semantics_from_code.post_cap_representation: _build_v2_hot_payload() output -- a condensed JSON object containing observation_id, acquisition_id, correlation_id, launch_mint, http_method, url, request_payload_sha256, response_status, response_data_present (bool marker), response_text_present (bool marker), response_headers_sha256, artifact_representation/digest/size_bytes/compressed_bytes, content_type, a narrow metadata subset (launch/purpose/provider/method/request_type/timestamp), and retained_at. Full response_data/raw_body_base64/response_text are absent.
part2_cap_semantics_from_code.schema_version_signal: schema_version is ALWAYS SCHEMA_VERSION_V2 (=2) in both full and hot payloads -- it does NOT change to indicate representation. The only reliable discriminator is payload shape: presence of the 'response_data_present' key (hot) vs its absence (full, which instead has the literal 'response_data' field).

restart_persistence.verdict: RESTART_CAP_PERSISTENCE_FALSE_BY_DESIGN (not merely unverified -- proven false by direct code inspection)
restart_persistence.reasoning: self._payload_bytes is a bare in-memory instance attribute with no backing store (no DB column, no file, no external counter). It is unconditionally initialized to 0 in __init__. There is no code path that reads a prior value from anywhere. A process restart therefore ALWAYS resets consumption to 0 by construction. This is stronger than 'unverified by test' -- it is a structural fact of the implementation. No test in the repository claims otherwise (grepped test_ra4_c3_bounded_writer_enforcement.py and test_ra4_retained_acquisition_shadow_activation.py for 'restart'/'persist' -- zero matches).

part8_bounded_post_cap_replay_check.disclosed_finding_this_step: the module-level _observation_from_payload() helper (used in RA4-C5's Part 8 simulation) does NOT correctly handle the hot-payload's TOP-LEVEL acquisition_id/correlation_id/launch_mint fields -- it only reads payload.get('metadata'), which is populated in full payloads but the hot payload stores a narrower metadata subset AND duplicates acquisition_id/correlation_id/launch_mint at the top level instead of expecting them nested. This produced None values when first tried against hot rows in this milestone; direct field access (payload.get('acquisition_id') etc.) was used instead and succeeded. This is a real, minor gap in that helper's hot-payload support -- not a data-integrity issue (the data itself is present and correct in the stored payload), and not a retirement blocker, but worth fixing before that helper is relied upon as a general-purpose replay path.

part9_hard_cap_accounting.note_on_consumed_bytes_after_transition: consumed_bytes (self._payload_bytes) only increments on FULL-payload writes -- hot-payload writes do NOT add to this counter (confirmed by code: _write_budgeted is only called with full_payload_bytes, and the hot-payload path bypasses budget accounting entirely per retain()'s structure at line 336-342). This is why consumed bytes crept up slowly post-transition (1065138273 -> 1067641552, +2503279 bytes) despite 2375 additional hot rows being written -- those hot rows contributed 0 to the cap counter; the small increase came from the handful of small full-payload rows that still fit in remaining headroom.

part9_hard_cap_accounting.representation_used_after_threshold: predominantly hot (2375/2380 post-transition rows), with intermittent full rows for sufficiently small payloads -- exact code-contract behavior, not overshoot
part9_hard_cap_accounting.classification_reasoning: Cumulative full-payload bytes never exceeded the 1,073,741,824-byte cap at any observed point. The pre-write gate correctly downgraded writes to hot payload once they would have exceeded remaining headroom. No atomic-final-write overshoot exists in this implementation (verified by code read, Part 2) and none was observed in production data. No accounting anomaly detected -- the slow post-transition growth in consumed bytes is fully explained by the code's own accounting rule (only full-payload bytes count) and is not evidence of drift or double-counting.

part10_restart_persistence.evidence: direct code inspection (Part 2) -- self._payload_bytes has no persistence mechanism and is unconditionally 0 at __init__. No production restart was performed to test this; none was needed given the structural code proof.
part10_restart_persistence.implication_for_retirement: this means the 1 GiB cap is a per-process-lifetime ceiling, not a genuine daily quota -- a future creator_funding_worker restart (for any operational reason) would reset consumption to 0 and the writer would resume full-payload writes from that point. This is a property of the CURRENT V2 implementation worth flagging for any future hardening work, but does not block legacy DB retirement, which depends only on whether V2's bounded behavior (cap+fallback) is proven to work AT ALL under real traffic -- which it now is.
